hook: A client asked me last week: My SA is only $20K at 32. Is that bad?
content:
A client asked me last week: My SA is only $20K at 32. Is that bad?

My honest answer: Yes and no.

Yes, because compound interest needs time. Every $1K you skip topping up at 32 is roughly $4K you don't have at 65 at SA's 4 percent floor.

No, because most 32-year-olds I meet have $0 in voluntary top-ups. You are already ahead of the average.

The fix is not panic. The fix is a $200/month standing instruction into SA RSTU until you hit the FRS. Two cups of bubble tea a week.

DM me CPF and I will send you the exact RSTU calculator I use with clients.

hook: I had a stammer growing up.
content:
I had a stammer growing up.

For years I thought that disqualified me from ever doing sales. Sales was for the loud guy at the front of the room.

Then I joined AIA and met my first client. Quiet, anxious, never met an FA before. He said: I am glad you are not the kind that talks over me.

That day I realised the best advisors are not the loudest. They are the ones who shut up first.

If you are an introvert wondering whether this industry is for you, hear me out: listening is the unfair advantage. Closing 1000+ clients later, I still talk less than half the meeting.

What is the one trait you thought disqualified you that turned out to be your edge?

hook: Your company group insurance is not enough. Here is the math.
content:
Your company group insurance is not enough. Here is the math.

Most group plans cover 12 to 24 months of salary on death. If you earn $6K/month, that is roughly $72K to $144K of coverage.

Now the gap: a 35-year-old with a kid and a mortgage typically needs 10x annual income in protection. That is $720K. Your group plan covers 10 to 20 percent of what you actually need.

Worse: when you leave the company, the cover is gone. You re-apply at 45 with a cholesterol flag and the premium triples. Or you cannot get cover at all.

The fix is simple: buy your own term plan while you are healthy and young. Pay it off by 65. Sleep at night.

Save this if you are still relying on group cover only.
why_it_works: Concrete numbers + cost-of-delay + named life-stage + save CTA. Authority pillar with a specific frame.

hook: Why I left engineering for financial advisory at 22.
content:
Why I left engineering for financial advisory at 22.

I was on the Global Engineering Programme at NUS. Top scholarship. Six-figure starting salary path. Every parent's dream.

Then I did the math no one tells you to do.

As a salaried engineer: $40 per hour, capped at maybe $80 per hour by year 10. Trade your hours for money. Always.

As an FA running a system: $750 per hour blended, by year 3. Build once. Earn forever.

The twist: the FA path is not a sales job. It is a $0-cost franchise. AIA hands you the brand, the products, the digital app, the back office. You bring the discipline.

I hit $145K in my first year as a uni Y1, part-time, 99 percent cold market. No magic. Just the system.

If you are a final-year student looking at the corporate path, ask yourself: do I want to trade my next 40 years for hours, or for outcomes?

DM me FRANCHISE if you want to see the actual numbers I ran in 2017.

hook: At 55, the most expensive mistake is choosing CPF Life Standard without doing the math.
content:
At 55, the most expensive mistake is choosing CPF Life Standard without doing the math.

Three options. Same name on the form. Very different lifetime payouts.

Standard: highest monthly income, lowest bequest. Best if you are healthy and have other estate plans.

Basic: lower monthly income, larger bequest. Best if leaving money to kids matters more than monthly cash flow.

Escalating: starts lower, grows 2 percent yearly. Best if you are worried about inflation eating your purchasing power past 75.

Most people I meet just tick Standard because it is the default. They never run the breakeven against their actual life expectancy and family situation.

If you are turning 55 in the next 24 months, do this: get a personalised CPF Life projection from the CPF Board, then sit with an FA who can show you the bequest and inflation impact in numbers.

DM me LIFE for the comparison sheet I use with my pre-retirement clients.
why_it_works: Specific decision point + 3 clear options + cost-of-default framing + tactical next step.

hook: The richest 1 percent are not smarter than you. They just rejected one specific path.
content:
The richest 1 percent are not smarter than you. They just rejected one specific path.

Good grades. Good job. Good salary. The script we were handed.

Here is the inconvenient truth: the system was designed to produce reliable workers, not wealthy owners.

If everyone became rich, who would do the work?

The top 1 percent are mostly business owners. They control 90 percent of global wealth. They got there by stepping off the conveyor belt early.

Two paths from here:

Stay on the belt. Trade time for money. Hit the ceiling around year 15.

Or step off. Build something that earns while you sleep. Take 5 years of friction for 30 years of compounding.

Not saying the first path is wrong. Just saying it is a choice. Most people do not realise they are choosing.

Which path are you on, and is it on purpose?

Slide 4: At 35 - OA $160K to $250K, SA $90K to $140K. If SA is below $90K, RSTU now while you can claim tax relief.

Slide 5: The compounding gap - $10K extra in SA at 30 becomes $33K at 65. Skipping it is not nothing. It is $23K of free money.

Slide 6: Action - 1) check your statement, 2) compare to these benchmarks, 3) set a recurring RSTU even if just $100/month, 4) revisit yearly.

Like proof I was not good enough.

That sting is what keeps 95 percent of advisors small.

Then I learned one shift: a no is not a verdict on you. It is data. A piece of information you did not have before.

Now when a prospect says no I ask: what would have to change for this to be a yes? Sometimes they tell me. Sometimes I get the next client referred from them three months later. Sometimes I just close the loop and move on.

The real failure is not the no. It is letting the no decide whether you make the next call.

hook: The cheapest CI plan you can buy is the one for your kid before they turn 1.
content:
The cheapest CI plan you can buy is the one for your kid before they turn 1.

Most parents I meet think CI cover for kids is unnecessary. Kids are healthy. Why pay?

Here is what changes the math:

1. Premiums for a 6-month-old are roughly 30 to 40 percent of the same plan at age 25. Lock in young, lock in cheap.

2. Once a child has any chronic flag (asthma, allergies, eczema documented), the premium loads or the plan excludes that condition. By primary 1 it is often too late for clean cover.

3. The plan transfers to your child as an asset at adulthood. Day one of working life they already have lifetime CI cover, paid up.

This is not about expecting your kid to fall sick. It is about giving them a financial head start you cannot give them later.

If your child is under 2, this is a 10-minute conversation worth having before their next medical check-up.

hook: Your first paycheck is the most leveraged dollar you will ever earn.

Not because it is the biggest. It is the smallest. But it has the longest runway.

My default split for a 23-year-old earning $3.5K take-home:

50 percent essentials and rent. Boring but necessary.

20 percent SRS top-up. Tax-deductible. Compounds tax-free until 62.

10 percent term and CI premium. Lock in cheap rates while you are healthy.

10 percent investing. ETF or savings plan, automatic.

10 percent guilt-free spending. Burnout is more expensive than discipline.

The goal is not to feel poor. It is to set the system once so you stop deciding every month.

Save this. The dollar you allocate at 23 is worth roughly 6x the dollar you allocate at 45.

hook: I closed a client this month from a meeting in 2018.
content:
I closed a client this month from a meeting in 2018.

I did what every advisor is told not to do: I stayed in touch anyway. Birthday text. Forwarded one article a year if it was relevant. Replied when she posted on LinkedIn. No pitch, ever.

6 years later she messaged: Hey Leo, my dad passed last month and I realised I have no idea what insurance my mum has. Can you help?

Not the biggest case I closed this year. The most instructive.

hook: An ILP is not insurance. It is investment with insurance bolted on.
content:
An ILP is not insurance. It is investment with insurance bolted on.

If no one said this to you when you bought yours, here is what to look for:

1. Cost of insurance rises with age. Inside an ILP it eats your investment unit value silently. Check the annual statement. The number is there if you know where to look.

2. The fund management fees are 1.5 to 2 percent on top of the underlying fund's own fees. Two layers.

3. Surrender in the first 5 to 10 years usually returns less than premiums paid.

This does not mean ILPs are bad. They work for specific cases: forced savings discipline, embedded protection a person would not buy separately, estate planning.

They are bad when sold as your main investment vehicle. For most 25 to 35 year olds with no warm-up to investing, term plus ETF will compound harder.

If you have an ILP and have never had it explained in plain numbers, dig out the statement. Read the cost of insurance line. Then decide.

DM me ILP and I will send the 5-question audit I run on every existing policy I review.

hook: If you are 55 and have not done a retirement income gap analysis, do this 10-minute exercise this weekend.
content:
If you are 55 and have not done a retirement income gap analysis, do this 10-minute exercise this weekend.

Step 1: Write down your current monthly spending. Round up.

Step 2: Multiply by 60 percent (the typical retirement spend ratio).

Step 3: Multiply that by 12 months and 25 years (life expectancy buffer).

That is your retirement nut.

Step 4: Sum your CPF Life monthly + any annuities + investment income at 4 percent withdrawal rate.

Step 5: Subtract step 4 from step 3.

That number is your gap.

Most pre-retirees I sit with have a $300K to $700K gap and never knew until they did the math.

The earlier you see the gap, the more options you have. SRS top-up, AIA Pro Lifetime Protector, downsize HDB, part-time consulting income, family income transfers.

If the number scares you, message me GAP and I will send a clean Excel version of this exercise.

Not a sales pitch. A diagnostic.

hook: Got your BTO ballot? Here are the 5 financial moves before key collection.
content:
Slide 1: Got your BTO ballot? 5 financial moves before key collection. Save now.

Slide 2: Move 1 - Lock in your mortgage rate intent. Floating vs fixed. SORA-pegged vs board rate. Different strokes for different income trajectories.

Slide 3: Move 2 - Top up SA before you wipe OA on downpayment. Once OA goes to housing it cannot come back. SA at 4 percent compounds while you wait for keys.

Slide 4: Move 3 - Mortgage Reducing Term Assurance (MRTA). Cheap term cover that decreases with your loan. Or stand-alone term that stays level. The level term is usually the smarter buy.

Slide 5: Move 4 - Joint income protection. If one partner is the higher earner, model what happens to the mortgage if their income stops for 6 months. Group cover is rarely enough.

Slide 6: Move 5 - Set up the legacy admin. CPF nomination, will, LPA. 2 hours of paperwork that your future self will thank you for.

Slide 7: Save this carousel. DM me BTO if you want the spreadsheet I use with my BTO clients to model the 30-year cashflow.

hook: Last week I almost gave up on a team member.

Then I did the activity audit instead.

Turned out she was making 60 percent of the dials, but spending double the average time per conversation, and not booking second meetings because she was over-explaining product.

The lesson I almost missed: when results stall, audit the system before judging the person.

If you lead a team and someone is struggling, do this before the hard conversation: pull their last 30 days of activity numbers. Compare to your benchmarks at each step. The bottleneck is almost never effort. It is one specific gear in the system.

Which team member do you owe an audit to before a verdict?

Which one are you building right now?

hook: Disability protection is the most under-bought, most-needed cover in Singapore.
content:
Disability protection is the most under-bought, most-needed cover in Singapore.

Not death cover. Not CI. Disability income.

The one that pays you a monthly income if you cannot work due to illness or injury.

Why under-bought:

1. Most people assume CareShield Life is enough. It is not. Max payout is roughly $662/month for severe disability. Try replacing your $5K salary with that.

2. Premiums look more expensive than term life because the probability of a long-term disability claim is higher than a death claim before 65.

3. Nobody talks about it because it is unsexy.

For a 35-year-old earning $6K, supplemental disability income cover that replaces 70 percent of salary costs roughly $40 to $60/month. Less than your phone bill.

If your monthly income disappears next month for 12 months, what breaks first: rent, mortgage, kids, or your savings?

Message me INCOME for the comparison between CareShield supplements and stand-alone disability plans.

hook: If your last policy review was over 24 months ago, you are due for one. Here is what a real review looks like.
content:
If your last policy review was over 24 months ago, you are due for one. Here is what a real review looks like.

Not the 15-minute call your old advisor calls a check-in.

A real review is 60 to 90 minutes and answers 6 questions:

1. Has your income changed by more than 20 percent since the last policy was written? Coverage probably needs to scale.

2. Has your family situation changed (married, kids, parents dependent)? Beneficiaries and bequest math change.

3. Are any of your existing policies underperforming projection? Bonus rates and ILP performance drift over time.

4. Have new product structures landed in market that better fit your goal? AIA refreshes plan menus every 18 to 24 months.

5. Are you maximising every available tax relief (SRS, RSTU, MA VC)? Annual reset.

6. Is the legacy admin clean (will, CPF nomination, LPA, beneficiaries on every policy)?

If any answer is no or unclear, that is what a real review covers.

DM me REVIEW and I will send the 6-question worksheet. No pitch. Use it with your existing advisor if you have one.

hook: Education endowment plans are not the only way to fund university.
content:
Education endowment plans are not the only way to fund university.

They are one option. Often not the best.

What they give you:
- Forced savings discipline
- Some guaranteed return (2 to 3 percent)
- A bonus return (2 to 4 percent, projected)
- A small life cover on the parent

What they take:
- 18 to 21 years of locked-in cashflow
- Lower returns than equity-based vehicles over 18+ years
- Surrender penalties if life forces you out

For a kid currently age 0, with a target of $80K in tuition by age 18, the alternatives:

A: Endowment plan. Pay around $300/month for 18 years.

B: Term life on parent + monthly contribution into a global equity ETF. Same outcome with usually 30 to 50 percent more capital at age 18, with flexibility.

C: SRS top-up by parent (tax-deductible) plus a separate education plan triggered closer to age 12 when the time horizon is shorter and capital protection matters more.

No one option is right for every family. But endowment by default is the wrong default.

DM me UNI for the 3-option spreadsheet I use with new-parent clients.
why_it_works: Challenges default thinking + specific 3-option compare + non-pushy + named DM keyword.

hook: Most advisors track the wrong number.
content:
Most advisors track the wrong number.

They track sales. Sales is a lagging indicator. By the time it is bad, you are 60 days behind.

The leading indicators are 3 numbers:

1. Books per week. How many net-new appointments did you book.

2. Meetings per week. How many of those actually showed.

3. Closes per week. How many became signed cases.

My team's targets:

- 8 to 12 books per week

- 5 to 7 meetings per week

- 1 to 3 closes per week

If books are low, the issue is prospecting volume or script.

If books are fine but meetings are low, the issue is qualification or pre-meeting nurture.

If meetings are fine but closes are low, the issue is fact-finding or product fit.

Diagnose the bottleneck weekly, not monthly. The fix is usually 1 specific thing, not a general try harder.

Which of your 3 numbers is the weakest right now?
why_it_works: Counter-intuitive opener + specific framework + diagnostic logic + question close.

hook: If you earn more than $80K a year and have not opened an SRS account, you are donating to IRAS.
content:
If you earn more than $80K a year and have not opened an SRS account, you are donating to IRAS.

SRS in 4 lines:

1. Contribute up to $15.3K/year. The full amount is deductible against your taxable income.

2. At an 11.5 percent tax bracket, $15.3K saves you roughly $1.76K/year. At 15 percent, $2.3K. At 19.5 percent, $3K.

3. The capital sits invested (your choice of stocks, bonds, ILPs, single-premium endowment). Earnings grow tax-deferred until withdrawal.

4. Withdraw after 62, only 50 percent is taxable. Spread over 10 years and most retirees pay close to zero on the way out.

The trade-off: locked until 62 (or pay 5 percent penalty + full taxation).

For anyone over 30 in a 11.5+ percent bracket with stable income, this is the cheapest tax move on the menu. Do it before December.

DM me SRS for the comparison between holding cash, equity ETFs, or endowment inside the SRS shell.

hook: If you have never sat down with an FA, here is exactly how to do your first one without getting sold.
content:
If you have never sat down with an FA, here is exactly how to do your first one without getting sold.

Step 1: Pick someone with referrals you can verify. Ask 2 of their existing clients what the experience was like. If they cannot offer references, walk.

Step 2: Set the agenda upfront. Tell them: 60 minutes, fact-finding only, no product pitch in this meeting. Any FA worth their time will agree.

Step 3: Bring documents. CPF statement, last 3 payslips, list of every existing policy with premium and sum assured. The conversation is 10x more useful when grounded in numbers.

Step 4: Ask 3 questions: what is the gap I cannot see, what would you do first if you were me, what is my biggest risk in the next 5 years.

Step 5: Walk out without buying anything. Say thank you, tell them you will reflect for a week. Real FAs are fine with this.

Step 6: Decide in your own time. If their analysis was useful, go back. If not, you got a free diagnostic.

Message me FIRSTMEET if you want a printable version of these 6 steps.

hook: Most pre-retirees plan to downsize their HDB. Few model what it actually unlocks.
content:
Most pre-retirees plan to downsize their HDB. Few model what it actually unlocks.

If you bought a 5-room in 2005 for $400K, it is likely worth $700K to $900K today. Downsize to a 3-room at $500K, you free $200K to $400K of net cash.

Where that money should usually go:

1. Top up the Retirement Account up to ERS. CPF Life payout for life climbs roughly $200 to $400/month per $50K topped up at age 65, depending on plan.

2. Single-premium retirement income annuity. AIA Pro Lifetime Protector or equivalent. Locks in lifetime income, hedges longevity risk.

3. A liquid bucket (3 to 5 years of expenses) in fixed income or T-bills. So you do not panic-sell during a market drawdown.

4. A risk bucket (10 to 20 percent of the freed capital) in equity for the 25-year tail you might still live.

The split depends on your CPF Life choice, your other income, and your bequest goal.

The move I see most often: the freed cash sits in a savings account at 0.05 percent for 3 years while the retiree decides. That is the actual cost.

DM me DOWNSIZE for the 4-bucket worksheet.
why_it_works: Specific scenario + 4-bucket framework + opportunity cost reframe + DM CTA.

hook: Fear makes you careful. Power makes you dangerous.
content:
Fear makes you careful. Power makes you dangerous.

Most people stay careful for 40 years.

Careful sounds responsible. Careful is what your parents called wisdom.

Careful is also why most people retire on $400K and call it enough because it has to be.

Dangerous is different. Dangerous moves first. Dangerous launches the project before it feels ready. Dangerous quits the safe job at 28 to build the asset that pays at 40.

Dangerous is not reckless. Reckless is no plan. Dangerous is plan and move.

The gap between careful and dangerous is usually 1 conversation, 1 commitment, 1 system.

Which are you defaulting to this week?
why_it_works: Sharp opening line + reframe of cultural defaults + memorable contrast + identity question.

hook: If your mentor has not closed a case in 18 months, they are not a mentor. They are a manager.
content:
If your mentor has not closed a case in 18 months, they are not a mentor. They are a manager.

There is nothing wrong with managers. They run the team admin, file the compliance, sign off the cases.

But the difference matters when you are 9 months in and stuck.

A manager will tell you to make more calls.

A mentor who is still in the field will pull up your last 5 fact-finds and show you the exact line where you lost the case. They will roleplay the objection live. They will sit in on your next Zoom and feed you the question through Whatsapp.

When you are picking a team to join, ask 1 question: when was the last time you closed a case yourself?

Not a trick question. Just a clarity question.

The people I learned the most from were the ones still doing the work alongside me. Not above me.

If you are an early FC and your mentor cannot show you their last 5 cases, you are paying tuition for a degree they have not earned in years.
why_it_works: Sharp distinction + concrete behavioural test + specific question to ask + recruitment angle.

hook: $5 a day at 22 becomes $1.2 million at 65.
content:
$5 a day at 22 becomes $1.2 million at 65.

At 7 percent compound. Every day. Every week. Every year.

That is a kopi and a kaya toast.

Most 22-year-olds I meet do not believe me until I show them the spreadsheet.

Then they say: I do not have $5 a day.

Fair. Most people do not.

But most people also have a $40 dinner once a week, a $15 GrabFood Tuesday habit, a $90 Netflix and Spotify and gym combined.

$5 a day is a re-allocation, not a sacrifice.

The trick is not the $5. The trick is the 43 years.

The earlier you start, the less you need.

The later you start, the harder the math gets.

No one is going to do it for you. Set the auto-debit. Forget about it.

Save this if you needed the reminder.

hook: I paid out my first claim in 2018. I learned more about insurance in that one week than in my first year of selling it.
content:
I paid out my first claim in 2018. I learned more about insurance in that one week than in my first year of selling it.

The client was 41. Stage 2 colon cancer. Treatable. Expensive.

We filed the CI claim. Money landed in 11 working days. No quibbles.

He did not have to take a single panicked call from the hospital billing desk. He did not have to ask his elderly parents for money. He did not have to break his fixed deposit.

The coverage was bought 4 years earlier. He paid roughly $80/month for it. The payout was $250K.

That ratio is what insurance is.

- A small cost most months you do not feel.

- A large cheque at the moment your life would otherwise restructure around money.

When people ask me what I do, I do not say I sell insurance. I say I make sure that when life punches you in the face, your bank account does not also fall over.

If you have been delaying a CI conversation, do this: imagine you get a diagnosis next month. Run the math on what your savings can absorb. The gap is the case for cover.
why_it_works: Specific dated case + cost vs payout numbers + identity reframe + scenario question close.

hook: At 55, you can withdraw money from your CPF. Most people do not realise the 4 ways this can backfire.
content:
At 55, you can withdraw money from your CPF. Most people do not realise the 4 ways this can backfire.

1. Withdrawing above the FRS threshold means your CPF Life payout drops. Permanent. The reduced payout is locked in for life.

2. The withdrawn cash, once outside CPF, no longer earns 4 percent guaranteed. Most retirees park it in a 0.05 percent savings account.

3. CPF Life monthly income is not subject to estate distribution issues. Cash outside CPF is. If your estate planning is messy, more cash outside CPF often means more friction at your passing.

4. The withdrawn cash becomes vulnerable to family pressure (kids' wedding, kids' BTO, kids' business). CPF inside the system is harder to give away under emotional pressure.

None of this means do not withdraw. There are valid reasons:

- You have ample alternative retirement income

- You want capital for a private investment with a clear plan

- You have a bequest goal that requires liquid assets

But the default of withdraw because I can is the most expensive default in pre-retirement.

DM me 55 if you want the 4-question framework I use with clients to decide what to keep, withdraw, or top-up at 55.
why_it_works: Counter-intuitive frame + 4 specific risks + balanced (when to withdraw) + named DM keyword.

hook: I want to be the boss of 100 people earning $10K/month by 2030.
content:
I want to be the boss of 100 people earning $10K/month by 2030.

Not $10K total. Each. Monthly.

That is the goal. Specific, dated, repeatable.

Most goal-setting in this industry is a vibe. Become a top performer. Build a strong team. Help people. The words feel right and the numbers are missing.

I write the goal as a sentence with all 4 elements: 100 people, $10K/month, by 2030, sustainably.

The sentence forces 4 sub-questions:

1. Where are these 100 people coming from? (Recruitment system.)

2. What does an FC at $10K/month look like? (Activity and case-mix benchmark.)

3. How long does it take to grow someone from intake to $10K/month? (12 to 24 months in our system.)

4. What breaks at 100 people? (Mentorship bandwidth, training infrastructure, culture fit at scale.)

The sentence is not a slogan. It is a 4-question audit I run on the business every quarter.

If your goal cannot survive being broken into 4 sub-questions, it is not a goal. It is a wish.

What is yours, in 1 sentence?
why_it_works: Specific BHAG + transparent breakdown + counter-intuitive principle + question close.

hook: The best advisors are not better salespeople. They are better educators.

The best advisors are not better salespeople. They are better educators.

A salesperson convinces.

An educator clarifies.

A salesperson hides discomfort.

A salesperson talks 70 percent of the meeting.

hook: You are not behind. You are just early in the season.
content:
You are not behind. You are just early in the season.

If you are 24 and feeling poor, broke, slow, behind everyone on Instagram who is buying a HDB, eating Omakase, traveling business class, you are seeing a curated highlight reel.

The people you are comparing yourself to:

- 80 percent are servicing debt that does not show on Instagram

- 15 percent are getting parental subsidy that does not show on Instagram

- 5 percent are genuinely ahead and they are usually not the loudest ones

Seasons in life:

22 to 30 is the planting season. Long hours, low rewards, compounding skills.

30 to 45 is the growing season. Visible progression, but built on what you planted earlier.

45+ is the harvesting season. The ones who skipped planting are still trying to plant.

Do not skip the planting season because the harvest takes a decade longer.

If you are tired right now, it is the right kind of tired. Stay in it.
why_it_works: Reframe of cultural pressure + specific stats + agricultural metaphor + permission close.

hook: If your only investment vehicle is a regular savings plan with the bank, you are paying the highest fees in the market.
content:
If your only investment vehicle is a regular savings plan with the bank, you are paying the highest fees in the market.

A typical bank RSP charges 1 to 2 percent sales charge per contribution + 1.5 to 2 percent annual fund management fee + you get a curated shortlist of funds, not the full universe.

A modern alternative for $500/month:

- A no-load global equity ETF (VWRA or IWDA + EIMI for emerging exposure)

- Held inside an SRS account (tax-deductible) or a CDP-linked broker (Tiger, Moomoo, IBKR)

- Total annual cost: 0.20 to 0.25 percent

Over 25 years on $500/month, the fee gap between 2.5 percent total cost and 0.25 percent costs you roughly $90K to $130K of compounded returns.

That is a flat in the Klang Valley, lost to fees.

This does not mean every advisor-recommended product is wasteful. There are good reasons to pay for advice (forced discipline, bundled protection, behavioural support, structured payouts).

But the default of bank RSP is rarely the right answer for a 30-year-old with a 30-year horizon.

DM me ETF for the 3-step setup I use with clients who want a passive core + advised satellite.
why_it_works: Specific cost gap + concrete alternative + opportunity-cost framing + balanced + DM CTA.

hook: Healthcare costs do not stop at 65. They start at 65. Here is what changes.
content:
Healthcare costs do not stop at 65. They start at 65. Here is what changes.

Until 65, your hospitalisation cover is usually paid via MA. Auto-debit, low friction, low awareness.

After 65:

- Premium typically scales 2 to 3x compared to age 50

- The MA balance you have built up has to fund both the rider portion and any catastrophic claim

- Some plans cap entry age, so switching providers at 67 is rarely an option

- Pre-existing conditions get harder to insure as they accumulate

The move at 55 to 60 is to stress-test your medical plan against a 25-year horizon:

1. Will my MA + cash buffer fund the rider for 25 years at projected premium hike?

2. Is my plan an Integrated Shield Plan with full ASR rider? If only Co-pay, what is the out-of-pocket on a Class A stay?

3. Is there a plan in market that better matches my hospital preference and budget?

4. Can I afford the rider lifetime, or do I drop it at 75 and accept higher co-pay?

None of these are dramatic. All of them are easier to address at 55 than at 75.

Message me HEALTH and I will send the 4-question diagnostic and the comparison sheet of the major IShield plans.
why_it_works: Specific age-bracket trigger + bullet pain points + numbered diagnostic + DM CTA.

hook: If your only saving is a 3 percent fixed deposit, you are losing 1 to 2 percent a year to inflation.
content:
If your only saving is a 3 percent fixed deposit, you are losing 1 to 2 percent a year to inflation.

Singapore's structural inflation runs around 2 to 3 percent. SG Core inflation has spent stretches above 4 percent recently.

A 3 percent FD at 3 percent inflation is a real return of zero. After tax, slightly negative.

This does not mean cash is bad. It means cash is a tool, not a strategy.

The 3-bucket frame I use with most under-30 clients:

1. Liquid cash bucket = 3 to 6 months of essential expenses. T-bills, fixed deposits, or money market funds. Kept against emergency, not against inflation.

2. Mid-term bucket = funds you will deploy in 1 to 5 years (BTO down payment, wedding, business capital). Short-duration bond funds, single-premium endowment, or stable allocation.

3. Long-term bucket = funds you will not touch for 7+ years. Equity ETFs, regular savings plans into diversified equity, plus your CPF SA quietly compounding at 4 percent.

When people complain about not making money, it is usually because they have all 3 buckets sitting in the first one.

Which bucket are you over-weighted in right now?
why_it_works: Counter-intuitive math + 3-bucket framework + diagnostic question. Clean Authority pillar.

hook: Knowing more products is not helping you close.

The close happens at the question, not the recommendation.

If the prospect cannot articulate the gap clearly themselves by minute 30 of the meeting, no amount of product depth will close them.

Go learn 5 plans deeply. Memorise 20 questions you can ask in any order.

The first list is technical. The second list is what actually moves the case.

hook: 5 money habits that separate clients who retire well from those who do not.
content:
5 money habits that separate clients who retire well from those who do not.

Not income. Not luck. Habits.

From 1000+ clients across 7 years:

1. They automate. Every contribution is auto-debit. SRS, RSTU, ETF, term premium. They do not decide every month. The system decides.

2. They name their accounts. Not Account 1 and Account 2. Kids' University. Mum's Hospital Fund. 2030 House Move. Naming changes how they spend it.

3. They review yearly, not monthly. Once a year, 90 minutes, all numbers in 1 sheet. Monthly checking creates panic. Yearly review creates discipline.

4. They do not chase the news. Markets drop, they do not move. Markets rip, they do not move. The plan was written when they were calm. They trust the plan.

5. They tell someone the plan. Spouse, FA, accountability partner. Plans you keep secret tend to die quietly.

None of these are sophisticated. All of them are durable.

Which 1 are you missing right now?
why_it_works: Universal tip + numbered list + counter-intuitive insights + concrete each + diagnostic question close.
